svg.aria-label: CausalVis architecture: video and masks are lifted to 3D object tracks; a language model reads the question and names the removed object; the counterfactual world builder replays the scene using the real video until the removal can reach an object and the world model after that; a collision check writes events to a store; the language model answers from the store.
svg.text: FLOW · ONE QUESTION FROM VIDEO TO ANSWER
also → 3D orbiting GIF of the predicted world

g.text: Brown = object outline from the video mask.
Dashed = outline our 3D guess would draw.
Move the camera until they overlap.
3 known shapes, one size, flat table.
So each object is just x, y (+ turn for cubes).
Turn is noisy per frame, so a physics rule
says: it only changes at collisions.
21% of videos have two look-alikes that
differ only by material: never mix them.
The model learns only V(gap), shared by
So A's push is always exactly −B's push:
momentum is conserved by the arithmetic,
friction learned per material, per frame:
This "leapfrog" order stays stable over long
runs. Momentum lost to friction is written
down as "given to the table", so it can be
checked. Spheres roll, so they slow least:
the model found that without being told.
decides: the world model's contact step
Every box an object fills is a "sensor". Where
two objects' boxes meet is the contact point.
The normal comes from the shape of that patch.
learns from: motion only, never answers
Start from a real moment, let the model run
20 frames by itself, measure how far off it is,
adjust, repeat. Voxel bounces run inside every
step: the direction is fixed geometry, the
strength can learn. 11,182 videos, laptop CPU.
decides: our rule + world model positions
sphere: would touch the cube at 50 → simulate
cylinder: was hit by the now-changed sphere.
rubber cube: enters at 51, real until the
decides: rule we wrote, tuned on validation

any pair not listed: no collision
Three copies of one world: a summary (.json),
every position of every frame (.npz, used for
the 3D GIF), and a plain-text version the
language model reads. All options of one
question are read from this same world.
1. Does this collision happen in the store?
2. If the question says "will NOT happen", flip it.
It does not choose when to simulate: the
question has no timing in it. On 60 test
questions: 86.2%, same as a plain lookup.
decides: the method, not the model
"no-sim" deletes the object and trusts the video.
The gap to 88.1% is what simulating adds.
